title: Build AI Systems for Discernment, Not Approval - Angel Ortmann Lee, Duolingo
talk_summary: A Duolingo security engineer shows that trained human reviewers rubber-stamped 50% of fake AI cheating flags, and that a copy change forcing them to find independent evidence before upholding a flag cut false acceptances by 21%. The broader lesson is that the human-AI interaction loop, not the model, determines whether you get real judgment or approval theater, and that every interaction is a label you should capture.

takeaways.technique: Force independent evidence before upholding an AI flag
takeaways.what_they_do: Proctors were told the AI signal is only a preliminary alert and they must find corroborating evidence in the video before upholding a flag, instead of a yes/no approval.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the AI signal is just a preliminary alert. They're the final decision-maker... they must find independent evidence
takeaways.numbers: 50% of fake signals accepted before; 21% increase in rejection rates after copy change

takeaways.technique: Split compound yes/no questions into separate signals
takeaways.what_they_do: Headphone detection asked one CTA that conflated 'did the model detect headphones' with 'is this a violation'; they split it so a correct detection (hearing aid) isn't logged as a false negative.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there's actually two questions hidden in this single, uh, single CTA

takeaways.technique: Capture the diff, not the binary accept/reject
takeaways.what_they_do: They note that if a human clicks yes then edits the output, logging only 'accepted' creates a false positive label; you must measure the diff between AI output and final result.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If you don't capture that diff... you actually capture a false signal that then can pollute your data sets

takeaways.technique: Agent as junior dev: plan, surface assumptions, break into reviewable PRs
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of giant one-shot diffs or per-file pings, the agent plans, asks good questions, documents design decisions, and splits work into meaningful reviewable chunks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want someone who's able to plan, ask good questions, and document those design decisions

takeaways.what_they_do: High-stakes decisions get deliberate review gates and friction; low-stakes chat is made frictionless. Friction is placed exactly where errors are costly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to build in friction exactly where the stakes are high

takeaways.technique: Design the interaction to yield labels, not just approvals
takeaways.what_they_do: Treat every human/agent interaction as a structured label source (assumptions rejected, tradeoffs overridden, follow-up questions) feeding the next iteration.
takeaways.evidence_quote: every interaction is already a label
